The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, covering various methods and their applications across quantum optics, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate. A unified overview is needed to relate different approaches.
method: The paper reviews and categorizes time-propagation techniques for non-Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting commonalities and differences within a unified framework.
result: It presents a comprehensive overview of simulation methods, including their applicability and limitations in different physical contexts.
conclusion: The unified framework helps researchers choose appropriate simulation techniques for non-Markovian dynamics, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical applications.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error-correction performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, ensuring 4-cycle-free Tanner graphs and deriving exact code rates. They also propose an encoding scheme and evaluate decoding with QBLNMS and layered binary sum-product decoders.
result: The proposed codes show nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder over depolarizing and Markovian channels, and require only one shared Bell pair for one family.
conclusion: The scalable constructions and improved decoding demonstrate practical potential for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that belief matching can significantly improve performance.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance depends on the measurement schedule, especially when measurements are noisy. The authors aim to optimize schedules for hardware with noisy readouts.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, using the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) to compare performance. They test repeating measurements and compare decoding with minimum-weight perfect matching versus belief matching.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance under measurement-biased noise but offers little benefit for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for optimizing dynamical codes with noisy measurements, emphasizing the importance of the teraquop volume and correlated-error decoding.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits by combining tensor network contraction with a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is limited by exponential overhead, restricting accurate simulation of large-scale circuits. The authors aim to extend the scale of exact sampling to validate quantum algorithms and assumptions.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit, enabling exact sampling from ideal and noisy circuits.
result: They demonstrate sampling from QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, achieving a scale previously out of reach.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, enabling validation of assumptions and conjectures at larger scales.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture on geometric speed limits for state preparation, showing that extrinsic curvature of control spaces can lead to violations.
motivation: The authors aim to test a conjecture that energy fluctuations during state preparation are lower bounded by the minimal geometric length of accessible protocols, which would have implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.
method: They analyze the conjecture using qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems, demonstrating counterexamples where the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: The conjecture is shown to be false in general; violations occur when the control space is curved.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit conjecture does not hold universally, and curvature effects must be considered in quantum control and thermodynamic bounds.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of QAOA parameter optimization for Ising models, proving structural properties and efficient algorithms for finding global optima.
motivation: Parameter tuning in QAOA is a bottleneck; the authors aim to show it is a structured signal-processing problem rather than a black-box search.
method: They prove the QAOA expectation is a partial Fourier series, derive bandwidth bounds, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and use a subdivision algorithm for global optimization.
result: They demonstrate polynomial-time global optimization for commensurable weights and concentration of optimal angles near zero for regular graphs, validated on RQAOA instances.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical foundations and practical algorithms that improve QAOA performance, with implications for quantum optimization.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for solving semidefinite programming problems, leveraging quantum singular value transformation and an inexact ADMM framework.
motivation: Large-scale semidefinite programs are computationally challenging due to costly linear system solves and eigenvalue decompositions; quantum computing offers potential speedups.
method: The authors develop an inexact ADMM framework that tolerates errors from block-encoding and quantum measurement, and use a polynomial proximal operator for semidefinite cone constraints, with quantum singular value transformation accelerating projection updates.
result: They prove convergence to an ε-optimal solution under strong duality and provide complexity analysis showing favorable scaling in dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: The QADMM algorithm demonstrates potential for solving large-scale SDPs more efficiently on quantum computers, though practical implementation remains challenging.

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates of quantum states, revealing a qualitative difference in state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental, and the role of imaginary coordinates has been unclear. The authors aim to provide a complete characterization of these constraints.
method: They derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, leading to a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space.
result: They uncover a surprising qualitative difference in the shape of the state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of imaginary coordinate constraints and highlights a dimension-dependent geometric feature of quantum state space.

title: Nisq In Practice: Navigating Noise, Scale, And Hardware Constraints Of Near-term Devices In Quantum Machine Learning Workflows
authors: Chisomo Daka And Somnath Bhattacharyya
abstract: The arrival of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices defines an era in which quantum utility is fundamentally constrained by finite coherence times, limited qubit counts, gate infidelities, restricted connectivity, and measurement noise. Within this regime, hybrid quantum-classical frameworks have emerged as the dominant operational paradigm, particularly for quantum machine learning (QML). This review identifies a fundamental trade-off between expressivity, trainability, and noise resilience that governs the performance and scalability of NISQ-era QML systems. To contextualize these challenges, we introduce the resource-constrained iterative routing framework, a hardware-aware conceptual architecture that integrates topology-aware classical compression and distributed quantum orchestration to maintain circuit depths within device-dependent limits while routing representations toward symmetry-constrained Hilbert subspaces to mitigate noise-induced barren plateaus. Furthermore, we shift the discussion of quantum advantage away from asymptotic fault-tolerant complexity toward the notion of operational NISQ advantage based on finite-resource scaling, trainability preservation, and sampling complexity. We evaluate the practical resource efficiency of variational quantum algorithms, quantum kernel methods, and quantum neural networks across superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and photonic platforms. The review also examines reproducibility challenges, emphasizing benchmarking against optimized classical baselines, and discusses strategies for managing the sampling overhead of error mitigation alongside distributed execution and quantum circuit compilation. Ultimately, NISQ in Practice positions hybrid QML as a physically constrained computational paradigm while outlining a pathway from contemporary noisy workflows toward early fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
tldr: This review analyzes the trade-offs in NISQ-era quantum machine learning, proposing a resource-constrained iterative routing framework to address noise, scalability, and hardware constraints.
motivation: NISQ devices are limited by noise and hardware constraints, and QML workflows need practical strategies to achieve quantum advantage despite these limitations.
method: The paper reviews variational quantum algorithms, quantum kernel methods, and quantum neural networks across various hardware platforms, and introduces a conceptual architecture integrating topology-aware compression and distributed orchestration.
result: It identifies a fundamental trade-off between expressivity, trainability, and noise resilience, and proposes the notion of operational NISQ advantage based on finite-resource scaling and trainability preservation.
conclusion: The review positions hybrid QML as a physically constrained paradigm and outlines a pathway from noisy workflows to early fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Constrained Quantum Optimization Via Iterative Warm-start X Y ...
authors: David Bucher, Maximilian Janetschek, Michael Poppel, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien And Sebastian Feld
abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a leading hybrid heuristic for combinatorial optimization, but efficiently handling hard constraints remains a significant challenge. -mixers successfully confine quantum state evolution to a feasible subspace, such as the Hamming-weight-1 sector for one-hot constraints. On the contrary, warm-starting biases the search toward promising regions based on preliminary solutions. Combining these two techniques requires maintaining the essential alignment between the initial state and the mixer Hamiltonian to preserve convergence guarantees. Previous work demonstrated warm-starting with -mixers via a biased initial state, but relying only on standard mixer Hamiltonians. Consequently, the initial state is no longer a ground state of the mixer. In this work, we overcome these limitations by formulating a warm-started -mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints and proving its ground-state properties. Furthermore, we provide a shallow circuit implementation suitable for NISQ implementations. We embed the warm-starting into a classical heuristic that iteratively updates the bias based on previous samples, called iterative warm-starting (IWS). Extensive numerical simulations on Max- -Cut and traveling salesperson problem instances demonstrate that IWS-QAOA significantly accelerates the solution-finding process, increasing the probability of sampling optimal solutions by orders of magnitude compared to standard XY-QAOA. Finally, we validate our approach on the ibm_boston QPU using hardware-tailored 144-qubit problem instances. By coupling IWS-QAOA with a greedy steepest-descent post-processing strategy to repair infeasible measurements caused by hardware noise, we successfully identify optimal solutions on actual quantum devices.
tldr: This paper introduces a warm-started XY-mixer for QAOA to handle one-hot constraints, proving ground-state properties and demonstrating significant speedups in finding optimal solutions on both simulations and a 144-qubit IBM quantum processor.
motivation: QAOA struggles with hard constraints, and existing warm-starting methods break the alignment between initial state and mixer, losing convergence guarantees. The authors aim to combine warm-starting with XY-mixers while preserving these guarantees.
method: They formulate a warm-started XY-mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints, prove its ground-state properties, and provide a shallow circuit implementation. They embed this in an iterative warm-starting (IWS) heuristic that updates biases based on previous samples, and test on Max-Cut and TSP instances, including hardware experiments with post-processing.
result: IWS-QAOA increases the probability of sampling optimal solutions by orders of magnitude compared to standard XY-QAOA in simulations, and successfully finds optimal solutions on the ibm_boston QPU with 144 qubits.
conclusion: The proposed warm-started XY-mixer effectively accelerates QAOA for constrained optimization, offering a practical approach for NISQ devices.

title: Resetting In A Viscoelastic Bath: The Bath Remembers
authors: Ion Santra And Debankur Das
abstract: We study stochastic resetting of a probe particle in a viscoelastic environment where only the probe is reset while the medium retains memory of its past dynamics. Using a minimal model with finite correlation time, we analyze the competition between the resetting timescale and the viscoelastic relaxation timescale. This interplay leads to nonequilibrium steady states that differ qualitatively from those of Markovian Brownian motion with resetting. In particular, strong memory effects produce stationary position distributions with non-exponential tails. For instantaneous resets, we derive the limiting steady-state distributions analytically and compute exactly the time-dependent leading non-vanishing moments. We also investigate non-instantaneous resetting via constant-velocity return protocols. In contrast to overdamped Brownian motion, where steady-state fluctuations are independent of the return dynamics, we find that in a viscoelastic medium the fluctuations depend on the reset velocity. This protocol dependence arises from the finite memory of the environment and highlights the role of environmental correlations in resetting-induced steady states.
tldr: This paper studies stochastic resetting in a viscoelastic bath, showing that memory effects lead to non-exponential steady-state distributions and protocol-dependent fluctuations.
motivation: To understand how environmental memory affects resetting-induced nonequilibrium steady states, which is relevant to information thermodynamics and stochastic processes.
method: The authors use a minimal model with finite correlation time, derive analytical results for instantaneous resets, and analyze non-instantaneous resetting via constant-velocity return protocols.
result: They find that strong memory effects produce non-exponential tails in stationary distributions, and that fluctuations depend on reset velocity, unlike Markovian Brownian motion.
conclusion: Environmental correlations play a crucial role in resetting-induced steady states, highlighting the need to consider memory in thermodynamic descriptions of such processes.

title: Linear-combination-of-unitaries Decomposition For The Laplace Operator

Specifically, Poisson problems augmented with periodic, Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, and mixed boundary conditions are considered on the unit interval and on higher-dimensiona…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012455] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides alternative linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) decompositions for discrete elliptic differential operators, specifically for Poisson problems with various boundary conditions.
motivation: The authors aim to improve quantum algorithms for solving differential equations by offering more efficient LCU decompositions for the Laplace operator, which is a key component in many quantum simulation tasks.
method: They derive LCU decompositions for the discrete Laplace operator under periodic, Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, and mixed boundary conditions on the unit interval and higher-dimensional domains, likely using spectral or finite-difference discretizations.
result: The paper presents new LCU decompositions that may reduce the number of terms or improve the scaling compared to existing methods, though specific numerical improvements are not detailed in the abstract.
conclusion: The work contributes to the toolkit for quantum algorithms for differential equations, but its direct relevance to the specified research interests is limited, as it focuses on algorithmic decompositions rather than information-theoretic or thermodynamic aspects.

[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014210] Published Fri Jul 31, 2026.

motivation: Rare system-wide resonances are expected to play a key role in the stability of the MBL phase, and new theoretical frameworks are needed to account for them.

result: They identify signatures of rare resonances and characterize their impact on the MBL transition.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the role of rare events in MBL, but it is primarily a many-body physics study without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics of information processing.

title: Fate Of Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions From Sudden To Slow Quench Limit
authors: Xiang Zhang And Fuxiang Li
abstract:
Author(s): Xiang Zhang and Fuxiang Li

Previous investigations of dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT) have predominantly focused on sudden quench protocols. In this work, we systematically explore the fate of DQPT from the sudden to the slow quench regime. We establish that DQPT remains robust under slow quenching when the protocol…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014320] Published Fri Jul 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the robustness of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPT) under slow quench protocols, showing they persist but with modified behavior.
motivation: Previous DQPT studies focused on sudden quenches; this work aims to understand DQPT in the slow quench limit, which is more experimentally relevant.
method: The authors systematically analyze DQPT for various quench protocols, likely using exact solutions or numerical simulations for specific models, and compare sudden vs. slow quench dynamics.
result: DQPT remains robust under slow quenching, but the critical times and scaling behavior change, with a crossover from sudden to adiabatic-like behavior.
conclusion: DQPT is a general phenomenon not limited to sudden quenches, but its characteristics depend on the quench rate, providing insights into non-equilibrium quantum dynamics.

title: Switching Characteristics Of Electrically Connected Stochastically Actuated Magnetic Tunnel Junction Nanopillars

[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014426] Published Wed Jul 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electrically coupled magnetic tunnel junctions with stochastic switching, modeling their collective behavior with a Markov chain to enable probabilistic spintronic hardware.
motivation: To understand and predict the behavior of coupled stochastic magnetic tunnel junctions, which could form the basis for probabilistic computing hardware.
method: The authors develop a Markov-chain model that predicts the collective behavior of coupled junctions from single-device measurements, and validate it against experiments.
result: They demonstrate that electrical coupling can realize tunable Ising-like interactions, and the model accurately captures the switching characteristics of the coupled system.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for probabilistic spintronic hardware, but it is more focused on device physics and applications rather than fundamental quantum information or thermodynamics.

We ben…

motivation: SVD provides a convenient Hermitian-like diagnostic for non-Hermitian many-body systems, but its reliability for locating MBL transitions is unclear, especially when time-reversal symmetry is present.
method: The authors benchmark SVD-based diagnostics against known MBL transitions in non-Hermitian systems with time-reversal symmetry, likely using numerical simulations of many-body models.
result: The study reveals limitations of SVD-based diagnostics in accurately identifying MBL transitions under time-reversal symmetry, suggesting they may be unreliable in such cases.
conclusion: SVD-based diagnostics should be used with caution for non-Hermitian MBL systems with time-reversal symmetry, and alternative methods may be needed.

title: Hilbert Space Fragmentation In A Driven-dephasing Rydberg Atom Array

abstract:

The model supports degenerate zero modes that form disconnected subspaces classified by a consecutive double excitation addressing operator, with the number of subspaces growing exponentially with chain length according to a modified Fibonacci recurrence.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032015] Published Tue Jul 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Hilbert space fragmentation in a driven-dephasing Rydberg atom array, revealing multiple long-lived metastable plateaus and an exponential growth of disconnected subspaces.
motivation: Understanding the emergence of long-lived metastable states in driven dissipative quantum systems is crucial for controlling quantum dynamics and potential applications in quantum information processing.
method: The authors model the driven-dephasing dynamics with an effective dephasing PXP model and analyze the structure of degenerate zero modes, classifying disconnected subspaces using a consecutive double excitation addressing operator.
result: They find that the number of disconnected subspaces grows exponentially with chain length according to a modified Fibonacci recurrence, leading to multiple metastable plateaus.
conclusion: The work provides insight into Hilbert space fragmentation in a realistic Rydberg system, which may inform future studies on quantum thermalization and control.

title: Berry-phase-induced Canonical Structure Of Quantum Fluctuations Across The Mott-superfluid Phase Diagram

We develop a unified field-theoretical description of the Bose-Hubbard model that captures low-energy dynamics across the insulator-to-superfluid transition. We show that commonly used cumulant expansions about the Mott ground state fail in the superfluid phase not only quantitatively but also funda…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033116] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a field-theoretic description of the Bose-Hubbard model across the Mott-superfluid transition, highlighting the role of Berry phase in quantum fluctuations.
motivation: To provide a unified low-energy description of the Bose-Hubbard model that correctly captures both the Mott insulator and superfluid phases, addressing failures of standard cumulant expansions.
method: The authors construct a field theory for the Bose-Hubbard model, incorporating Berry phase effects and analyzing quantum fluctuations across the phase transition.
result: They show that cumulant expansions fail in the superfluid phase and that Berry phase induces a canonical structure for quantum fluctuations, leading to a unified description.
conclusion: The work offers a new theoretical framework for the Bose-Hubbard model, with implications for understanding quantum phase transitions and fluctuations.

motivation: Understanding how frustration and disorder shape relaxation in complex systems is central to statistical physics and quantum annealing, with implications for quantum computing hardware.

motivation: The spectral form factor is a key diagnostic of quantum chaos, and understanding its behavior in many-body systems is important for characterizing thermalization and chaos.

result: They obtain explicit expressions for the spectral form factor up to second order, revealing universal features and symmetry-class dependencies.
conclusion: The results provide a deeper understanding of quantum chaos in many-body systems and may have implications for the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis and related phenomena.

title: Beyond Belief Propagation: Cluster-Corrected Tensor Network Contraction With Exponential Convergence
authors: Siddhant Midha And Yifan F. Zhang

Systematic corrections to belief propagation enable polynomial-time tensor network contraction algorithms while providing rigorous bounds on approximation errors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033010] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review of space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their relation to quantum computation.
motivation: To provide a unified view of dynamical evolution in quantum many-body systems by treating space and time on equal footing, avoiding complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories.
method: The review discusses the discretization of time evolution in lattice systems, emphasizing space-time duality and its connection to brickwork quantum circuits, drawing analogies with digital computation.
result: The paper presents a pedagogical framework that unifies various approaches to quantum many-body dynamics through space-time duality, highlighting the role of brickwork circuits.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful perspective for understanding quantum dynamics, with implications for quantum simulation and computation.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and metastable phases.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems, which may lead to novel quantum phases.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear driving and mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution.
result: Highlights mechanisms for metastable superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders in photoexcited Mott insulators.
conclusion: Photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators offer a rich platform for exploring quantum metastable phases, but the paper is a review without new technical results.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, focusing on time-optimal and noisy rearrangement algorithms.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, efficient and robust atom rearrangement is crucial, but existing algorithms lack open-source implementations and noise robustness.
method: The authors develop the atommovr simulation framework and study three settings: time-optimal noiseless rearrangement, noisy rearrangement with realistic error models, and noiseless dual-species rearrangement. They extract lower bounds, compare strategies, and propose a novel dual-species algorithm called InsideOut.
result: The framework provides lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identifies advantageous strategies under different error regimes, and the InsideOut algorithm achieves near-unity success in avoiding blocked configurations.
conclusion: atommovr serves as a community tool for benchmarking and developing rearrangement algorithms, lowering the barrier for experimental groups and stimulating progress in minimizing atom loss.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model, providing a new example of ergodicity breaking in higher dimensions.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in dimensions higher than one, and finding exact examples is important for understanding ergodicity breaking.
method: The authors study a 2D quantum gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in the XY model, and use the duality to map them to scars in the gauge model.
result: They demonstrate that the exact QMBS of the XY model become exact QMBS of the dual gauge model, providing a versatile construction for higher-dimensional scars.
conclusion: The work offers a new method to find QMBS in higher-dimensional models, potentially advancing the study of non-thermalizing states.

title: Visualizing The Effect Of Engineered Internal Perturbations On An Artificial 2d Atom And Explaining It Using Perturbation Theory
authors: Marco Weiss And Franz J Giessibl Fabian Stilp
abstract: Atomic orbitals are affected by external perturbations, such as the proximity of other atoms or exposure to electric or magnetic fields, that induce Stark and Zeemann splittings. The thought experiment: What would happen with these orbitals if one would position a fraction of a positive elementary charge with a tweezer at about half the atomic radius? This would allow for a highly controlled experiment on the alteration of atomic orbitals by a perturbation. Such a tweezer does not exist, so this remains a thought experiment. However, we can achieve something similar in an artificial 2D atom such as a quantum corral where we put single adsorbate atoms inside, which can be engineered by lateral manipulation with scanning probe microscopy. We show that the perturbation potential qualitatively follows the one between two natural atoms, a long-range attraction followed by a short-range repulsion. We demonstrate the state-selectivity of the short-range interaction leading to tunable electronic states. Surprisingly, long-range Coulomb attraction can be detected experimentally, even though charges are strongly screened on the metal surface. We estimate an effective charge of the adsorbate on the order of 1/1000 of an elementary charge. The perturbed orbital is imaged by atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy and described by perturbation theory. As a practical application, this introduces the ability to tune the geometry of the reactivity of an artificial atom, similar to the change in the chemical reactivity of a natural atom, when it is bound to other atoms.
tldr: This paper uses scanning probe microscopy to perturb a quantum corral (artificial 2D atom) with adsorbates, visualizing and explaining the resulting orbital changes via perturbation theory.
motivation: To experimentally simulate the effect of a point charge on atomic orbitals, which is not possible with real atoms, by using a quantum corral as an artificial atom.
method: They place single adsorbate atoms inside a quantum corral using lateral manipulation with scanning probe microscopy, then image the perturbed orbitals with AFM and STM, and model the results with perturbation theory.
result: They observe state-selective short-range interactions and long-range Coulomb attraction, estimating an effective charge of ~1/1000 of an elementary charge, and demonstrate tunable electronic states.
conclusion: The work provides a way to tune the reactivity of artificial atoms, analogous to chemical bonding in natural atoms, and offers insights into perturbation effects in confined systems.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review covers tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution, a technique in nanoscale optical imaging.
motivation: To provide an overview of tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy, which combines scanning probe techniques with optical fluorescence to achieve superresolution at the atomic scale, useful for studying molecules and their structures.
method: The paper is a review article summarizing the techniques and applications of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy, including the use of a scanning tip as a nanoscale optical antenna.
result: The review discusses how this technique achieves atomic-scale resolution and reveals electronic and vibronic properties of molecules, submolecular structures, and reactions.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy is a powerful tool for nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy, with potential for further insights into molecular systems.

abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications, including magnetism, topology, and dynamics.
motivation: To summarize the rapidly evolving field of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials, which has revealed new phenomena and challenged theories.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes current knowledge on magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials, including experimental and theoretical advances.
result: The review highlights new phenomena such as topological magnetism, nonequilibrium dynamics, and Floquet effects, and discusses potential applications.
conclusion: The field of 2D van der Waals magnets is expanding, offering new insights into magnetism and promising directions for future research and applications.
